content.text: Procedural abstraction allows programmers to use procedures knowing only what they do, not how. Software libraries take this idea one step further — they are entire collections of pre-written, pre-tested procedures that any programmer can use in their own programs without having to write those procedures from scratch. Libraries are one of the most important practical tools in real-world programming.

content.definition: A collection of procedures that may be used in creating new programs. Simplifies the task of creating complex programs by providing pre-written, tested code.

content.text: The use of libraries simplifies the task of creating complex programs. Tasks like sorting, searching, image processing, encryption, and network communication require complex algorithms that would take days or weeks to write and test from scratch. Libraries provide these capabilities as ready-to-use procedures — call the procedure, get the result.

Existing code segments can come from internal or external sources, such as libraries or previously written code. Understanding where code comes from helps you know how to use it, how to acknowledge it, and whether you can trust it.

rows: Internal source
Code you or your team wrote previously in the same project or a past project
A procedure you wrote last week that you want to reuse in a new program
Acknowledge if written by a teammate rather than yourself
External source — library
A collection of procedures provided by a third party
A math library, image processing library, or network library
Read the API documentation; acknowledge the library in your program documentation
External source — previously written code
Code found online, in a textbook, or provided by another developer
A code snippet found in a tutorial or open source repository
Acknowledge the origin and original author's name in documentation

content.definition: A specification for how the procedures in a library behave and can be used. Documentation for an API is necessary to understand the behaviors provided and how to use them.

content.text: An API is the contract between a library and its users. It specifies: what procedures the library provides, what parameters each procedure takes, what each procedure does (its behavior), and what value each returns. The API does NOT reveal how the procedures are implemented internally — that is hidden by procedural abstraction.

rows: Software Library
A collection of pre-written, tested procedures available for use in new programs
A hardware store full of tools you can buy and use
API
A specification describing how to use the procedures in the library — what they do, what inputs they take, what they return
The instruction manual for each tool in the store
API Documentation
The written reference material explaining every procedure in the library
The detailed guide that explains exactly how to use each tool correctly and safely

content.text: Documentation for an API/library is necessary in understanding the behaviors provided by the API/library and how to use them. Without documentation, you cannot know what procedures are available, what parameters they expect, what they return, or what happens in edge cases. Even if you could guess the procedure names, you would not know the exact behavior — and guessing wrong leads to bugs.

rows: What procedures are available
sortList(aList), searchList(aList, target), reverseList(aList)
What parameters each procedure takes and their expected types
sortList takes one parameter: a list of comparable values
What each procedure returns
sortList returns a new sorted list; does not modify the original
What happens in edge cases
sortList on an empty list returns an empty list; sortList on a list of one element returns that same list
Any constraints or requirements
searchList requires the list to be sorted; if unsorted, behavior is undefined

content.label: Key Idea
content.text: Using a library is procedural abstraction in action. You use the library's procedures knowing only WHAT they do — not HOW they work internally. The API documentation tells you everything you need to know to use the procedures correctly. This is exactly why documentation for an API is necessary — without it, you cannot use the library correctly even if you have access to it.

Without libraries, every programmer would have to solve the same problems over and over. With libraries, a problem solved once can be shared and reused by thousands of developers. This is the practical realization of the benefit of using existing correct algorithms as building blocks.

rows: Sort a list of names
Write and test a sorting algorithm from scratch — hours of work
Call sortList(names) — one line, instantly correct
Process an image
Write pixel manipulation algorithms from scratch — days of work
Call resize(), crop(), filter() from an image library
Encrypt a password
Implement cryptographic algorithms from scratch — expert-level complexity
Call encrypt(password) from a security library
Make a network request
Write low-level socket connection code
Call get(url) or post(url, data) from an HTTP library
Generate a random number
Implement a pseudo-random number generator algorithm
Call RANDOM(a, b) — built into the AP CSP reference sheet

content.label: Exam Tip
content.text: The AP exam tests four specific things about libraries: (1) A software library contains procedures that may be used in creating new programs. (2) Existing code segments can come from internal or external sources such as libraries. (3) The use of libraries simplifies the task of creating complex programs. (4) An API is a specification for how the procedures in a library behave; documentation is necessary to understand and use them.
Summary: What to Know for the Exam

items: A software library is a collection of procedures that may be used in creating new programs
The use of libraries simplifies the task of creating complex programs
Existing code segments can come from internal sources (your own previous code) or external sources (libraries, previously written code by others)
An API (Application Program Interface) is a specification for how the procedures in a library behave and can be used
Documentation for an API/library is necessary to understand the behaviors provided and how to use them — without it you cannot use the library correctly
Using a library is procedural abstraction — you use its procedures knowing only what they do, not how they work internally
Code from external sources must be acknowledged in your program documentation including the origin or author
